'And in the forty-fifth jubilee in the second week and in the second year, Judah took for his first-born Er, a wife from the daughters of Aram, named Tamar' — Jubilees' framing of the Judah-Tamar narrative with the canon's typical chronological-jubilee structure. The verse demonstrates Jubilees' distinctive editorial method: re-narrating Genesis with jubilee-week timestamps. Tewahedo chronological tradition preserves this jubilee-counting as a way of dating biblical events.

candidates.draft_body:
Jubilees (Ethiopian tradition) Book of Jubilees (Mäṣḥafä Kufāle) (c. 150 BC)

'And in the fifth year Tamar was reckoned unto Onan, his second son, that he should take her, and Onan said: I will not give my seed to my brother, the seed of Tamar — and the Lord slew him before my face for the wickedness which he did, and slew Onan also for the same' — Jubilees preserves Onan's sin of refusing to raise up seed for Tamar (Gen 38:9). Tewahedo doctrine on the obligation of the brother-in-law to raise up seed for the dead brother (the yǝbäm or levirate-relative obligation) finds canonical anchor here: the obligation is so weighty that its refusal is named alongside the worst-category covenant violations. The Tewahedo modern canonical-pastoral practice of supporting widows from within the extended family draws warrant from this passage.

'And Tamar conceived, and she bore twin sons; and she called the name of the one Perez, and the name of the other Zerah' — Jubilees follows the Gen 38 narrative of Perez and Zerah. The Tewahedo Christological-genealogy tradition: Perez is the ancestor of David (Ruth 4:18-22 = Mt 1:3) and ultimately of Christ. Tamar — the Canaanite-presumed-prostitute-daughter-in-law — preserves the Davidic-Messianic line through her courageous-faithful action where Judah faltered. The Tewahedo Marian-typology tradition reads Tamar (with Rahab, Ruth, Bathsheba, and Mary) as the four-women-in-the-Messianic-genealogy, each receiving canonical-pastoral honor as faithful-female-link-in-the-Messianic-line.

'And we showed to Judah that he should not seek her any more, because of the judgment of the Holy of holies; and Tamar was acquitted, and she became more righteous than he. And he had relations with her no more' — Judah's confession 'she is more righteous than I' (Gen 38:26) is preserved with explicit divine ratification: Tamar is canonically vindicated, Judah is canonically rebuked. Tewahedo penitential canon reads this as the canonical pattern for the confession-of-the-stronger-sinner-against-the-weaker-victim: Judah's straightforward acknowledgment 'she is more righteous than I' is the model formula for confession when the wronged party turns out to be canonically-just. The Tewahedo confessor's näsḫa-of-acknowledgment formula draws verbal anchor here.
